# Solution Concept & Originality

Advising customers on mobility subscriptions involves two requirements that have to be addressed by the same system. The recommendation has to be numerically accurate, but its reasoning also needs to be understandable to the customer. These requirements are better suited to different technologies. Deterministic methods can provide reliable calculations, while generative language models are useful for explaining results in natural language. Our solution combines both approaches without letting either compromise the other. The system is built on a FastAPI and PostgreSQL service layer, deterministic pricing and scoring engines, a LangGraph agent for the conversation, a university-hosted GPT endpoint, and Langfuse for prompt management and tracing. Chapter 3 describes how these fit together.

A central design decision that distinguishes this system from a standard retrieval-augmented assistant is the separation between determining results and communicating them. The deterministic engines decide what is true, and the language model is only permitted to decide how it is said. This separation is particularly important in the context of financial advice. A fabricated or incorrect figure that sounds plausible can be more problematic than providing no figure at all, since the customer may not be able to identify the error when making a decision. We therefore established the invariant that the language model never produces a number that reaches the user. Every euro, kilogram and minute is computed deterministically and handed to the model as fixed context it may only narrate or explain. Where the model does contribute to a forecast, it predicts how often someone will travel, never what that travel costs, and the trip counts it produces are priced by the same engine as everything else. The customer's three onboarding priorities are resolved into the weights that every ranking uses, so a stated preference is not a cosmetic setting but part of the calculation.

The same principle applies to the actions that the model is allowed to perform. No portfolio change is written to the database until the agent has received explicit confirmation from the customer. An incorrect tool call can therefore not directly cancel or modify a subscription. This design is also relevant from a regulatory perspective. Article 14 of the EU AI Act requires systems to allow effective human oversight and intervention, while Article 50 requires users to be informed when they interact with an AI system. Our prototype is unlikely to fall under the high-risk classification, since recommendations for mobility subscriptions are not included in the categories listed in Annex III. Nevertheless, the interaction model follows the general principle of keeping the final decision under human control. The agent can propose and simulate changes, but the irreversible action requires confirmation from the customer. Because this confirmation is enforced by the control flow rather than by the prompt, the guarantee holds regardless of how the model behaves.

What makes this more than a textbook agent example is that its output can be checked. Because the engines are deterministic, their results are reproducible and can serve as the reference against which a naive single-call implementation is measured, which is what Chapter 6 reports. Tutorial agent systems typically give the model as much scope as possible. We took the opposite approach and examined for each subtask whether a language model was necessary at all. For pricing, eligibility and scoring the answer was no. This restraint is what makes the system measurable in the first place.
